title: Easy exam 3
about: Ten single-choice questions on the basics: one concept each, with the classic look-alike options.

questions.title: Becoming another user
questions.text: Which command opens an interactive session as the user `ana`, loading her environment as in a new login?

options.t: `su ana`
options.why: It opens a session as ana, but without the `-` it does not load her login environment (the current directory and most of your variables stay).

options.t: `su -c ls ana`
options.why: `-c` runs a single command and returns; it is not an interactive session.

options.t: `su - ana`
options.why: The `-` makes `su` load the environment of the user it switches to.

options.t: `sudo ana`
options.why: `sudo` runs the command given as argument as another user; `ana` is not a command.

questions.title: Script outside the PATH
questions.text: You are in `/home/ana`. The script `backup.sh` has execute permission and is in `/home/ana/scripts`, a directory that is not in the `PATH`. Which command runs it?

options.t: `backup.sh`
options.why: Without a slash the shell looks only in the `PATH`: "command not found".

options.t: `./backup.sh`
options.why: `./` means the current directory, `/home/ana`, where the script is not: "No such file or directory".

options.t: `scripts/backup.sh`
options.why: A relative path with a slash is used as it is, without searching the `PATH`.

options.t: `/scripts/backup.sh`
options.why: It starts at the root of the tree: `/scripts` does not exist.

questions.title: From line 3 onwards
questions.text: The file `f` has six lines, `a` to `f`, one per line. What does `tail -n+3 f` print?

options.why: That is `tail -n 3 f`, the last three lines.
`tail` never prints the beginning of a file; that would be `head -n 2 f`.
`-n+3` means "from line 3 to the end".
Only one line would be printed by `sed -n 3p f`; `tail -n+3` goes on to the end of the file.

questions.title: Permissions on a directory
questions.text: Which statement about the permissions of a directory is TRUE?

options.t: With `r` on a directory you can enter it with `cd`.
options.why: Entering needs `x`; `r` is for listing the names.

options.t: With `x` on a directory you can list its names with `ls`.
options.why: Listing the names needs `r`; `x` is for traversing it.

options.t: To create a new file inside a directory you need `w` on that directory.
options.why: Creating or deleting entries changes the directory itself, which is what `w` controls.

options.t: With `w` on a directory you can read the contents of the files inside it.
options.why: Reading a file depends on the permissions of the file; `w` on the directory is about its entries.
Without braces the shell reads the name `n0`, not `n` followed by `0`.
`$n0` is the variable `n0`, which is empty and disappears; `${n}0` is `3` followed by `0`.
`$n0` is expanded, to nothing; only single quotes would print it literally.
`$n0` is not `$n` followed by a `0`; it does not give `3`.

questions.title: Overwrite and append
questions.text:
What does this print?
```
echo a > g
echo b >> g
echo c > g
cat g
```

options.t: `a`, `b`, `c` on three lines
options.why: The last `>` truncates the file before writing.

options.t: `a` and `c` on two lines
options.why: Only `>>` keeps what was there before, and the last command uses `>`.
`>` empties `g` each time; the last command leaves only `c`.

options.t: `b` and `c` on two lines
options.why: `echo c > g` removes the earlier lines, including `b`.

questions.title: Partition table limits
questions.text: Which statement about MBR and GPT partition tables is TRUE?

options.t: MBR allows up to 128 primary partitions, while GPT allows only 4.
options.why: The other way round.

options.t: GPT allows up to 128 primary partitions, while MBR allows only 4.
options.why: One of the reasons GPT was created.

options.t: GPT works only with the legacy BIOS, and MBR only with UEFI.
options.why: GPT goes with UEFI and MBR with the legacy BIOS.

options.t: MBR supports larger partitions than GPT, up to 256 TB.
options.why: The limits are the other way round: about 2 TB for MBR and 256 TB for GPT.

questions.title: Ctrl+Z
questions.text: `sleep 300` is running in the foreground and you press Ctrl+Z. What happens?

options.t: It is suspended, not finished: `jobs` lists it as stopped and `bg` or `fg` resumes it.
options.why: Ctrl+Z only pauses the process and returns the prompt.

options.t: The process is terminated and removed from the system, exactly as with Ctrl+C.
options.why: Ctrl+C aborts the command; Ctrl+Z only suspends it.

options.t: The process keeps running, but now in the background so the prompt is free.
options.why: It is paused, not running; it needs `bg` to continue in the background.

options.t: The process is moved to the foreground of a new shell opened for it.
options.why: Nothing is created: you get the prompt of the same shell back.

questions.title: Finding commands
questions.text: Which statement about how the shell finds a command is FALSE?

options.t: A command typed with a slash in it, like `bin/tool`, is not searched in the `PATH`.
options.why: True: it is used as a path.

options.t: `echo $PATH` prints the directories in which the shell searches, separated by `:`.
options.why: True.

options.t: The shell goes through the directories of the `PATH` in order and runs the first match.
options.why: True.

options.t: An executable in the current directory can always be run by typing just its name.
options.why: False: the current directory is searched only if it is in the `PATH`; otherwise you need `./name`.

questions.title: mv into a directory
questions.text: `notes` is a file and `docs` is an existing directory. Which statement about `mv notes docs` is FALSE?

options.t: The file `notes` ends up inside the directory as `docs/notes`.
options.why: True: an existing directory as destination receives the file.

options.t: `notes` no longer exists in the current directory.
options.why: True: `mv` moves, it does not copy.

options.t: The directory `docs` is replaced by a file called `docs`.
options.why: False: `mv` never replaces a directory by a file; it moves the file inside it.

options.t: If `docs/notes` already existed, it would be overwritten.
options.why: True: `mv` replaces a file of the same name without asking (unless `-i` is used).
